claims.text: High-entropy alloys resist simultaneous wear and corrosion through rapid, continuous formation of a self-healing passive oxide film.
The alloy's chemical complexity enables oxide-forming elements to segregate locally at mechanically exposed surfaces.
Local segregation of oxide-forming elements regenerates a protective surface film.
The regenerated passive film mitigates both abrasive damage and corrosive degradation.
A diversified HEA composition produces significant lattice distortion.
The initial HEA has a homogeneous distribution of oxide-forming elements.
Mechanical wear intermittently removes the surface film.
High configurational entropy drives rapid segregation of oxide-forming elements to freshly exposed areas.
Segregated oxide-forming elements rapidly re-establish the passive film after wear removes it.
The re-established passive film resists subsequent mechanical abrasion.
The re-established passive film resists subsequent corrosive attack.
The proposed HEA will have lower mass loss than the baseline during combined wear and corrosion.
The proposed HEA will have smaller wear scars than the baseline during combined wear and corrosion.
The proposed HEA will form fewer corrosion pits than the baseline during combined wear and corrosion.
The improvement in combined degradation resistance will exceed the simple additive effects of separate wear and corrosion resistance.
The protective mechanism operates under moderate wear and corrosive conditions that permit passive-film regeneration.
The protective effect may fail under extreme mechanical loads that overwhelm film regeneration.
The protective effect may fail in highly aggressive corrosive environments that overwhelm film formation.
